fallbackFor: Grok 4.6 timed out on the first planning phase; the owner authorized Opus 5 OAuth whenever Grok has an issue
summary: Opus 5 OAuth fallback single-pass planning audit of docs/security/supply-chain-policy.md and docs/research/source-catalog/adoption-ledger.json. The policy is a genuinely strong draft: dispositions are enumerated, production entry is restricted to `retain`/accepted `adopt`, the GSAP containment rule is explicit and narrow, and the ledger keeps every `unselected`-identity source at codeUseAllowed:false with a named stop gate, kill switch, and cannotOwn list that preserves Page IR, candidate, approval, and release separation. Visual-authoring expansion is correctly NOT authorized: Puck stays evaluate/no-code, GSAP carries expansionStatus blocked plus an explicit motion-builder prohibition, and R3F is blocked. That said, the packet cannot yet carry a safe implementation ticket. One P0: `adapt` is a production-reaching disposition with no required ledger entry, no named reviewer, no written clean-room record, and no CI-detectable artifact, while thirteen shortlist rows already hold adapt/learn dispositions with zero ledger coverage. Seven P1s follow: ledger entries omit most of the policy's own nine mandatory fields yet four assert codeUseAllowed:true, contradicting the policy's explicit forcing rule; there is no machine-readable ledger schema or field vocabulary, so the required CI check "reject invalid state combinations" is unimplementable and fails open on absent fields; GSAP is simultaneously codeUseAllowed:true and releaseUseAllowed:false with no defined build-versus-release or generated-site redistribution boundary; no outbound distribution model is declared anywhere, which makes every license-compatibility determination undecidable; hosted third-party services and subprocessors (OpenRouter and the upstream model providers behind SC-NPM-002) are an entirely missing supply-chain class; "build actions" are in the policy's applies-to scope but have no controls at all; and the ledger's declared planningDispositionAuthority does not cover four of its twelve entries. Blocked, evaluate, research, and license-review states are correctly walled out of production builds by the disposition rule plus codeUseAllowed:false, so containment on those classes holds. Model review is input only; nothing here substitutes for deterministic evidence, named humans, or independent verification.

findings.sectionOrLines: Policy 'Dispositions' (adapt clause, 'Only `retain` and an accepted `adopt` entry may enter a production build'); 'Repository and copied-code controls'; 'CI and release enforcement'; ledger entries[] (no adapt entries except SC-GH-005)
findings.issue: `adapt` is defined as a disposition whose clean, project-owned output MAY enter a production build, but no control makes that path detectable or gated. Nothing requires an adopt-equivalent ledger entry before adaptation, no named human reviewer or written provenance/license receipt is mandated, no clean-room record artifact is defined, and every CI enforcement bullet targets dependency, lockfile, SBOM, manifest, model/asset hash, or packaged-content surfaces that clean-room adapted source does not touch. Meanwhile the declared disposition authority (github-starred-one-box-shortlist-2026-08-29.md) already assigns adapt or learn-and-adapt dispositions to at least thirteen sources (t3code, ollama, deepagents, loop.js, buzz, chrome-devtools-mcp, ego-lite, hyperframes, astryx, Instatic, open-seo, strix, supermemory) and the ledger contains no entry for any of them.
findings.risk: The policy's stated objective is that nothing enters ONE BOX because it is popular, model-recommended, or technically convenient. `adapt` is precisely that door: an implementation ticket could lift architecture, protocol, state-machine, and envelope patterns from thirteen ungated upstream projects into production source with no ledger entry, no license receipt, no named approver, and no CI signal, including from sources whose license posture is unresolved. Provenance and attribution obligations would be discharged on assertion alone, and the failure would be invisible to every check the policy specifies.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: State in the Dispositions section that no `adapt` work may begin or merge without its own accepted ledger entry carrying exact upstream commit, license file receipt, named reviewer and date, clean-room boundary statement, and linked ticket; add a CI enforcement bullet requiring every PR that cites an adapt source to reference an accepted ledger ID; and add ledger entries (codeUseAllowed:false) for every shortlist row currently holding an adapt or learn-and-adapt disposition.

findings.sectionOrLines: entries[] SC-NPM-001..SC-NPM-004 vs policy 'Required ledger fields' items 1-9 and the forcing sentence 'An `unselected` revision, unavailable license, missing integrity, missing owner, missing oracle, or unresolved P0/P1 forces `codeUseAllowed: false`'
findings.issue: The policy mandates nine field groups per entry. Every ledger entry omits most of them: no publisher/maintainer, no acquisition channel, no requested filesystem/network/browser/model/secret/process/data/user-interaction permission set, no integrity or provenance evidence, no upstream maintenance posture, no vulnerability or upgrade owner, no support window or emergency response, no qualification oracle, no sandbox, no data class, no telemetry behavior, no named owner, no decision date, and no review expiry. `ownerTicket` is a ticket string, not the required human owner. Despite missing owner, missing integrity, and missing oracle, SC-NPM-001 through SC-NPM-004 all assert codeUseAllowed:true, which the policy's own forcing rule says is impossible.
findings.risk: The ledger is designated the product-level gate, yet its four code-use-true entries violate the exact rule that is supposed to make code use false. An implementer or a CI author can reasonably conclude that missing mandatory fields are tolerated for anything already in the tree, which reintroduces grandfathering-by-assertion — the same pattern the policy explicitly disclaims when it says the GSAP containment rule 'is not a general grandfathering path'. Absent review expiry, no retain decision ever lapses.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Either populate the missing mandatory fields for the four codeUseAllowed:true entries, or flip them to codeUseAllowed:false pending completion; and add an explicit `retain` backfill deadline plus reviewExpiry, owner, and decisionDate to every entry so the forcing rule and the entries agree.

findings.sectionOrLines: Ledger schemaVersion/entries[] field vocabulary; policy 'CI and release enforcement' bullet 'parse the adoption ledger and reject invalid state combinations'
findings.issue: No machine-readable schema, required-key list, or enumerated value vocabulary exists for the ledger. license.status alone takes five undefined ad-hoc values across entries ('clear', 'research-verified', 'scope-review-required', 'mixed-open-core-review-required', 'unavailable-license-file', 'per-model-and-conversion-review-required'), none of which the policy defines or maps to its disposition set. `releaseUseAllowed` and `expansionStatus` appear on exactly one entry (SC-NPM-004), so their default when absent is undefined. identity.type takes 'npm-lock', 'git-commit', and 'unselected' with no declared grammar, and identity uses both `package`/`version` and a `packages` map.
findings.risk: The single most important CI check the policy requires cannot be written deterministically, and the obvious implementation fails open: an entry that simply omits `releaseUseAllowed` or misspells a license status would pass. A gate whose vocabulary is undefined is a gate that silently degrades to a documentation file, while the authority manifest continues to point at it as the control on code use.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add a versioned JSON Schema next to the ledger enumerating required keys, allowed disposition values, allowed license.status values, identity grammar per type, and explicit fail-closed defaults for absent `releaseUseAllowed` and `expansionStatus`; reference it from the policy's CI enforcement section.

findings.sectionOrLines: entries[] SC-NPM-004 (codeUseAllowed:true, releaseUseAllowed:false, boundedUse 'Existing deterministic motion behavior already in the repository'); policy 'Dispositions' pre-policy retain containment paragraph
findings.issue: GSAP 3.15.0 is simultaneously cleared for code use and denied release use, but neither file defines the boundary between a production build and a release, nor states where GSAP output may appear. ONE BOX generates and publishes client websites; the entry does not say whether GSAP code is confined to the operator-facing application or is emitted into generated client site output. The policy's containment paragraph forbids the item being 'newly distributed' and forbids Release 1 clearance, while the ledger's codeUseAllowed:true offers no mechanism preventing the compiled artifact from reaching a client deliverable.
findings.risk: GSAP's Standard no-charge license is scope-dependent and explicitly unreviewed here, with licenseReviewerRole recording that no person is named and no acceptance is inferred. If existing motion code is emitted into generated or published client sites, distribution is already occurring under a license nobody has read against this use, and the ledger's own release block would be silently bypassed by the build. No deterministic check distinguishes the two cases.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add an explicit distributionScope field to SC-NPM-004 stating whether GSAP output is confined to the ONE BOX operator UI and never emitted into generated or published client sites; define build-versus-release in the policy; and if generated-site emission cannot be ruled out from the tree, set codeUseAllowed:false pending the named licensing owner's written scope decision under OBX-P175.

findings.sectionOrLines: 'License stop rules'; 'Repository and copied-code controls'; 'Policy objective' ('compatible license')
findings.issue: The policy repeatedly requires a 'compatible license' and lists stop conditions for commercial-use and redistribution ambiguity, but never declares ONE BOX's own outbound distribution and deployment model. It is not stated whether the product is hosted SaaS, a distributed desktop application, source delivered to clients, or generated sites redistributed to third parties — and the authority manifest records ADR 0002 target desktop/cloud topology as only `proposed`, meaning the model may change.
findings.risk: License compatibility is a function of the outbound distribution model. Without declaring it, no reviewer can decide the GSAP scope question, the PostHog open-core boundary, MPL-2.0 file-level source obligations, or any future copyleft or source-available candidate. Every license determination in the ledger rests on an unstated premise that a topology change would invalidate, and the license stop rules cannot be applied consistently by two different reviewers.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add a 'Distribution model' subsection to the license stop rules declaring the current outbound model for the application, worker images, and generated client site output, and state that a topology or distribution change reopens every license determination in the ledger.

findings.sectionOrLines: Policy 'Applies to'; 'Models, datasets, and custom code'; 'Hosted scripts, fonts, media, and assets'; ledger entries[] SC-NPM-002
findings.issue: The policy covers packages, repositories, generated code, skills, plugins, MCP servers, model weights, images, modules, build actions, deployment adapters, and hosted scripts — but not third-party hosted services and subprocessors that receive data at runtime. SC-NPM-002 ledgers the AI SDK and OpenRouter provider packages, yet OpenRouter is a hosted routing service and the upstream model providers behind it are further subprocessors; neither has a ledger entry. No control requires terms-of-service review, data-retention and training-on-customer-data terms, region and residency, subprocessor disclosure, incident notification obligations, availability commitments, or an exit and data-return path.
findings.risk: The highest-risk data egress in the system — client and prompt content routed to an aggregator and onward to unnamed model providers — sits outside the supply-chain policy entirely. The entry's stopGate mentions retention but nothing binds the vendor side, and a provider or subprocessor change upstream would trigger no review. This is also the class most likely to carry contractual and privacy obligations that the package-level license receipt cannot address.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add a 'Hosted services and subprocessors' section requiring, per service, the terms version, data classes sent, retention and training-use terms, region, subprocessor list, incident notification, availability and degraded mode, kill switch, and exit path; and add a distinct ledger entry for OpenRouter as a service with codeUseAllowed:false until those fields exist.

findings.issue: The applies-to line explicitly scopes build actions, but no section of the policy states any control for CI/CD supply chain: no requirement to pin third-party GitHub Actions to full commit SHAs, no default workflow token permission posture, no rule on secret exposure to third-party actions, no treatment of pull_request_target or fork-triggered workflows, no runner provenance requirement, and no review path for workflow file changes. The CI section describes only checks the pipeline must run, never the trust properties of the pipeline running them.
findings.risk: The enforcement mechanism is itself an unreviewed executable supply chain. A mutable third-party action tag, an over-permissioned workflow token, or a fork-triggered workflow with secret access can compromise builds and releases and can also disable or forge the very ledger, SBOM, and packaged-content checks the policy relies on. The enforcement ticket cannot be written safely without these requirements.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add a 'Build and CI supply chain' section requiring full-SHA pinning of third-party actions, least-privilege default workflow permissions, an explicit rule for fork-triggered workflows and secret access, runner provenance, and review ownership for workflow file changes.

findings.sectionOrLines: top-level planningDispositionAuthority; entries[] SC-GH-001 Puck, SC-GH-002 Electron, SC-GH-003 Yjs, SC-GH-004 LiveKit
findings.issue: The ledger declares github-starred-one-box-shortlist-2026-08-29.md as its planning disposition authority, and the catalog README states that for starred repositories only the 18-item shortlist assigns planning dispositions and phases and that no other document may add, promote, or reclassify a source. The supplied shortlist contains no row for puckeditor/puck, electron/electron, yjs/yjs, or livekit/livekit — LiveKit appears only in an exclusion note about livekit/agents. The ledger nonetheless assigns each a disposition, phase, bounded use, and stop gate, and cites no alternate authority for them.
findings.risk: Four of twelve entries carry dispositions that their declared authority does not grant. Either the ledger is adding candidates in violation of the catalog rule, or the planningDispositionAuthority pointer is wrong for these entries and their true provenance is unrecorded. Both readings break the traceability chain the authority manifest depends on when it says 'The shortlist owns planning dispositions; the adoption ledger and phase gates control any code use', and both make it impossible to tell who accepted these four dispositions.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: For each of the four entries, either cite the specific accepted document that assigns its disposition in a per-entry dispositionAuthority field, or add the corresponding rows to the shortlist under its stated selection rule; do not leave the top-level pointer covering entries it does not contain.

findings.issue: The value is not a valid SPDX license expression (SPDX requires the uppercase operator 'AND'), so it will not parse in any SPDX-aware tool the enforcement ticket adopts. Separately, the entry records no source obligations for the MPL-2.0 component even though policy required-field 4 mandates recording 'source obligations' and MPL-2.0 carries file-level source disclosure duties on modification and distribution. The entry also does not identify which package carries which license.
findings.risk: A license-scanning gate silently fails to evaluate the entry, and the MPL-2.0 disclosure obligation is unrecorded. The obligation is currently low-impact because the tooling is test-scoped, but it becomes material under any distribution model that ships these components — which is itself undeclared (see SC-P1-004).
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Change the value to a valid SPDX expression, attribute each license to its specific package, and record the MPL-2.0 source-disclosure obligation and the condition under which it would be triggered.

findings.sectionOrLines: entries[] SC-GH-005 identity.commit 'd026163f586d' vs SC-GH-008 identity.commit 'a1869ccfe73a829c3724f0a3570ab4c0b62bb33d'
findings.issue: The policy requires recording 'the exact upstream commit' and required-field 3 requires an exact commit, tag, digest, or hash. SC-GH-005 records a 12-character abbreviated hash while SC-GH-008 records a full 40-character hash, so the ledger is internally inconsistent on identity precision.
findings.risk: An abbreviated hash is not a full identity: it cannot be verified against a repository without ambiguity handling, is not collision-resistant in the way the policy's integrity language assumes, and defeats a CI check that would compare recorded identity to a fetched object. Since SC-GH-005 is the packet's only `adapt` entry, its provenance precision matters more than most.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Record the full 40-character commit SHA for SC-GH-005 and require full-length commit identifiers in the policy's required-fields section.

findings.issue: Six entries record their license receipt as the free-text string 'technology source catalog' rather than a file path, upstream LICENSE file reference, commit, reviewer, or date. The policy's required-field 4 demands 'the reviewer/date/receipt', and the repository-controls section requires recording 'the exact upstream commit and license file'. By contrast SC-HF-001 does cite a concrete document path, showing the ledger can express this.
findings.risk: A receipt that names a folder rather than an artifact is not verifiable and cannot be checked by CI. If an upstream project relicenses or a LICENSE file is found to conflict, there is no recorded snapshot to compare against, and no reviewer or date to hold the determination.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Replace each free-text receipt with the upstream LICENSE path at the pinned commit plus the reviewing human and date, matching the pattern already used by SC-HF-001.

findings.sectionOrLines: Policy 'Dispositions' (`blocked` vs `evaluate`); ledger entries[] SC-GH-002 Electron (decision blocked, phase 'E0/E4 research', killOrRemoval 'Discard out-of-tree spike'), SC-GH-006 R3F (decision blocked, phase 'post-Phase-1 ExperienceModule research')
findings.issue: The policy defines `blocked` as a state where a named gate 'prevents retained use' and `evaluate` as 'isolated research or benchmark only'. Two entries are marked `blocked` while simultaneously carrying a research phase, a bounded research use, and — for Electron — a removal plan that presupposes an existing out-of-tree spike. The policy's browser section similarly forbids only 'retained' desktop or remote-content browser packages before the EB plan passes.
findings.risk: The boundary between blocked and evaluate is undefined for isolated spikes. A reader could conclude that `blocked` still permits out-of-tree Electron or WebGL experimentation, which is precisely the activity the rejected embedded-browser plan and EB-001 hostile-page isolation gate are meant to hold. Production containment itself is intact — codeUseAllowed is false and the production-entry rule admits only retain and accepted adopt — so this is ambiguity rather than leakage.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: State explicitly in the Dispositions section whether `blocked` permits isolated out-of-tree research and, if it does not, either move these entries to `evaluate` with their gates intact or remove the research phase and spike language from the blocked entries.

findings.issue: Several standard package-ecosystem controls are absent: no dependency-confusion or internal-scope-reservation rule, no typosquat or name-similarity check, no minimum-age or quarantine window for newly published versions, no maintainer-change or ownership-transfer signal, no registry-provenance or signature verification requirement (npm provenance attestations are never mentioned despite the policy demanding 'integrity/provenance evidence'), and no policy for unmaintained or end-of-life packages.
findings.risk: The named controls cover what a dependency does once installed, but not how a malicious or hijacked version arrives. The dominant real-world npm compromise patterns — account takeover pushing a fresh patch version, and dependency confusion against an internal scope — would pass every check the policy currently lists.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Add bullets requiring internal scope reservation, registry provenance or signature verification where available, a quarantine window before adopting newly published versions, and a maintainer-change review trigger.

findings.sectionOrLines: 'Package and lockfile controls' (SBOM and vulnerability bullets); 'CI and release enforcement'
findings.issue: The SBOM requirement names no format, no storage location, no retention period, no signing or attestation, and applies only to release candidates, so no baseline inventory exists to diff the first release against. The vulnerability bullet defines a qualitative response posture but no severity rubric, no remediation time bounds, no named security owner, and no rule for a vulnerability with no available fix. The status line says 'enforcement ticket required' but no ticket ID for that work appears in either file, and none of the ledger ownerTickets (OBX-P140/150/160/170/175/180/185) is identified as it.
findings.risk: SBOM diffing — the control that detects unexpected inventory change — has no first term, and the vulnerability response has no clock or owner, so 'severity, exploitability, reach, fix availability' becomes a discretionary judgment with no accountable human. The unnamed enforcement ticket means the packet's own required next step has no addressable identity.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Name the SBOM format, storage, and retention; require a baseline SBOM at policy acceptance; add a severity rubric with remediation time bounds and a named security owner role; and assign an explicit ticket ID for the enforcement work in the policy status line.

findings.sectionOrLines: 'License stop rules' ('cannot be ... converted into a model-generated derivative' vs 'clean-room pattern extraction remains allowed'); ledger entries[] SC-GH-008 agent-native boundedUse
findings.issue: Two adjacent rules conflict for the same item class. `needs-license-review` items may not be converted into a model-generated derivative, yet clean-room pattern extraction from public documentation remains allowed. SC-GH-008 (agent-native, unavailable-license-file) has boundedUse 'Learn action-schema, grounding, and approval-hook patterns only' — exactly the activity both rules describe. In a repository where implementation is performed by models that have read the upstream source, no operational test distinguishes permitted clean-room extraction from a forbidden model-generated derivative.
findings.risk: The strictest license control in the policy has no decidable test in this project's actual authoring model. A reviewer can justify either conclusion for the same work product, which converts a fail-closed rule into a discretionary one for precisely the entries whose licenses are unresolved.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Define the operational boundary explicitly — for example, requiring that clean-room extraction for `needs-license-review` items proceed only from published documentation with a recorded statement that upstream source was not in the authoring context — and state which artifact records that determination.

findings.sectionOrLines: entries[] ownerTicket values across SC-NPM-001, SC-GH-007, SC-GH-008 (all OBX-P150); SC-GH-003/SC-GH-004 (both OBX-P170); SC-GH-001/SC-NPM-004 (both OBX-P175)
findings.issue: Single tickets own multiple unrelated entries spanning different phases and categories — OBX-P150 covers a current-baseline build dependency, an E8 analytics license review, and an E1 agent-runtime license review. The policy's workflow requires an implementation ticket per accepted item and states that a decision applies only to the exact identity and bounded role.
findings.risk: Per-item traceability weakens: closing a shared ticket can appear to resolve unrelated stop gates, and the CI check comparing dependency changes to accepted ledger entries cannot use the ticket as a discriminator.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Split shared ownerTickets so each ledger entry references a ticket scoped to its own gate, or add a per-entry gateTicket field distinct from the phase-level owner ticket.

findings.sectionOrLines: 'Skills, plugins, MCP, and agent tools' ('Every retained integration has a product kill switch that does not require the dependency to be healthy'); ledger SC-NPM-001 killOrRemoval
findings.issue: The kill-switch requirement is stated in absolute terms for 'every retained integration' but sits in the skills/plugins/MCP section, while build-time dependencies cannot have a runtime kill switch. SC-NPM-001's killOrRemoval is correctly a rebuild-and-repin path, not a switch, so the ledger and the policy sentence read inconsistently if the sentence is taken globally.
findings.risk: Minor. A CI check written from the policy sentence could demand a runtime kill switch for compile-time dependencies and either fail spuriously or be silently waived, eroding the check's credibility.
findings.smallestSafeCorrection: Scope the sentence to runtime and external-effect integrations, and state that build-time dependencies satisfy it with a documented repin-and-rebuild removal path.

acceptedStrengths: Production entry is restricted by an explicit rule — only `retain` and an accepted `adopt` may enter a production build — and every research, evaluate, adapt, needs-license-review, and blocked entry in the ledger carries codeUseAllowed:false, so those five states are correctly walled out of production builds.

Bounded GSAP use does not authorize visual-authoring expansion: SC-NPM-004 sets expansionStatus blocked, releaseUseAllowed false, cannotOwn includes 'visual motion authoring expansion' and 'human visual approval', and the stop gate names motion-builder and expanded visual authoring as prohibited without written scope consent.

The pre-policy retain containment rule is written narrowly, names GSAP 3.15.0 as its only current application, and states outright that it is not a general grandfathering path — an unusually disciplined way to handle an inherited license ambiguity.
licenseReviewerRole for GSAP explicitly records that no person is named and no acceptance is inferred, which resists the common drift of treating a role reference as an approval.

Every ledger entry carries a cannotOwn list that consistently preserves separation of Page IR and site-document authority, candidate identity, human approval, membership, qualification, and release — including for LiveKit (invitation, candidate lock, membership) and screenshot-to-code (HTML source, candidate, release).
The policy states that the lockfile, adoption ledger, and SBOM are three distinct inventories and none substitutes for the others, which is the correct framing and is frequently gotten wrong.

Puck is held at evaluate behind synthetic Page IR fixtures with a stop gate requiring proof of no alternate document or persistence authority, so the canvas-reference path cannot become a second document authority.

The models and datasets section correctly treats community conversions as independent supply-chain items requiring their own publisher, revision, license analysis, and hashes rather than inheriting the base model's license.

trust_remote_code, custom operators, pickled artifacts, and conversion scripts are confined to an isolated research worker until approved — the right default for the highest-risk executable class in the model path.

No model, plugin, or skill may hold approval, membership, release, deployment-credential, or risk-acceptance authority, and model quality explicitly never grants tool, mutation, approval, or release authority.
Vulnerability and license tool failures must report BLOCKED rather than PASS, which closes the standard fail-open hole in scanner-based gates.

Tool selection is deliberately left to the owning ticket with coverage, false-positive handling, egress, version, and replacement path recorded first — an honest deferral rather than a fabricated toolchain commitment.
Exceptions require an expiry, an independent reviewer, and a removal ticket, with no permanent exception and no model-authored acceptance valid.
The incident procedure correctly states that restoring service does not close the incident or waive provenance repair.

Packaged-artifact controls name concrete forbidden contents (repository history, sites/, .one-box/, secrets, browser profiles, audit scratch, developer home paths), which is specific enough to become a real check.

The policy holds the line that no retained desktop or remote-content browser package is allowed before the rewritten EB-001 through EB-021 plan passes, consistent with the authority manifest's `rejected` classification for the embedded browser domain.
missingEvidence: Bash is disabled in this session and no file-read, glob, or grep tool was available, so I could not verify either per-file SHA-256 (36db1f3c... and 5fff9caa...) or the stated target aggregate SHA-256 7403fc97f4b6a21c30fb708ad50ebe232868f90fd76fee9fb495bf1d833e08a0 against the working tree. The aggregate's derivation rule is also not stated in the packet. All findings rest on the supplied packet bytes as presented; packet integrity is unverified.

package.json and package-lock.json were not readable, so the ledger's identity claims are unverified: tailwindcss 4.3.3, ai 7.0.64, @openrouter/ai-sdk-provider 3.0.0, playwright 1.62.1, @axe-core/playwright 4.13.0, and gsap 3.15.0. Their license.receipt values point at package-lock.json, so the receipts themselves are unchecked. The packet's own note that 'current semver ranges resolve to exact package-lock.json versions' is likewise unverified.

Whether GSAP output is emitted into generated or published client site output, or is confined to the ONE BOX operator-facing application, could not be determined from the repository. This is the deciding fact for SC-P1-003 and I did not infer it.

Whether puckeditor/puck, electron/electron, yjs/yjs, and livekit/livekit appear in the 133-item starred snapshot could not be checked (github-starred-2026-08-29.json was not in the packet), so I could not distinguish 'ledger added starred candidates outside the 18-item shortlist' from 'these are non-starred sources whose disposition authority is simply uncited'. SC-P1-007 is written to hold under either reading.

The referenced supporting documents were not supplied or readable and their existence is unverified: docs/plans/one-box-master/06-technology/technology-adoption-roadmap.md, docs/research/source-catalog/hugging-face-one-box-candidates-2026-08-29.md, docs/research/source-catalog/one-box-technology-adoption-matrix-2026-08-29.md, docs/research/source-catalog/github-starred-one-box-relevance-2026-08-29.md, and docs/security/local-api-threat-model.md.
No ticket system access, so OBX-P140, OBX-P150, OBX-P160, OBX-P170, OBX-P175, OBX-P180, and OBX-P185 could not be confirmed to exist, to be open, or to carry the gates the ledger attributes to them.

No legal or license review evidence of any kind is available to me. I did not evaluate the GSAP Standard no-charge license terms, the PostHog open-core boundary, MPL-2.0 obligations, or the agent-native license status as legal conclusions; findings address only whether the packet records the required receipts and reviewers.

No CI, workflow, SBOM, scanner, or build-output evidence was accessible, so no claim in this review asserts what the pipeline currently does or does not enforce. The .github/workflows/ci.yml modification shown in git status was not inspected.
No runtime, test, vendor, or user-research evidence was accessible; none is invented anywhere in this review.

This is an Opus 5 OAuth fallback review under owner authorization after a Grok 4.6 timeout. It is model review and therefore input only. It is not Grok evidence, and it does not substitute for deterministic verification, a named human licensing owner, or independent review.

phaseDecision.reason: One P0 and seven P1 findings. The P0 is structural: `adapt` is a production-reaching disposition with no mandated ledger entry, no named reviewer, no clean-room record, and no CI-detectable surface, while thirteen shortlist rows already hold adapt or learn-and-adapt dispositions with zero ledger coverage — which reopens the exact door the policy objective closes. The P1s prevent a safe implementation ticket from being written at all: the ledger contradicts the policy's own codeUseAllowed forcing rule on all four code-use-true entries, there is no ledger schema or field vocabulary so the required CI parse check is unimplementable and fails open, GSAP's build-versus-release and generated-site redistribution boundary is undefined against an unreviewed scope-dependent license, no outbound distribution model is declared so no license determination is decidable, hosted services and subprocessors are a wholly missing class covering the system's largest data egress, build actions are in scope with no controls, and four of twelve entries have dispositions their declared authority does not grant. Containment of blocked, evaluate, research, and license-review states out of production builds does hold, and the GSAP-to-visual-authoring expansion boundary is correctly closed, so the packet is not unsafe on those axes — it is incomplete and self-contradictory on the axes that would govern the enforcement ticket. The P2 and P3 items are bounded follow-ups and are not independently blocking.

nextActions: Resolve SC-P0-001 first: require an accepted ledger entry with exact commit, license file receipt, named reviewer and date, and clean-room boundary statement before any `adapt` work begins, add the corresponding CI enforcement bullet, and create codeUseAllowed:false ledger entries for every shortlist row currently holding an adapt or learn-and-adapt disposition.
